--- title: "Functional connectivity" subtitle: "Seed-to-target correlation and seed-regressor GLM from spatial ROI extraction." jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: auto --- Seed-based functional connectivity asks a simple question: which target regions co-vary with a chosen seed region once nuisance signals are removed? This page starts from a spatial `neuroim` object, extracts named ROIs, and then builds the analysis from the same pieces used for a GLM: a dataset that owns its timing, a nuisance model, the `residualize` projection, and `fmri_lm` itself. The input is already preprocessed. Motion correction, registration, spatial normalization, and denoising decisions happen upstream. This tutorial begins at the point where an aligned four-dimensional image and its regions of interest are ready for modeling. ## Define and extract the spatial ROIs The synthetic image below has a non-identity signed affine and 160 time points. The seed drives two target regions at different strengths; a control region shares only a nuisance signal. `cuboid_roi` defines each region on the image grid. `series_roi` returns an `ROIExtractionResult`, not an anonymous array. ::: {#1d0c753e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import neuroim as ni import fmrimod as fm from fmrimod import baseline_model, design_matrix from fmrimod.residualize import residualize from fmrimod.spec import covariate from fmrimod.stats import seed_target_correlation, seed_target_lm rng = np.random.default_rng(13) n_time = 160 spatial_shape = (7, 6, 5) affine = np.array( [ [-2.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0], [0.0, 2.0, 0.0, -6.0], [0.0, 0.0, 2.5, -5.0], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0], ] ) space_3d = ni.NeuroSpace.from_affine(affine, spatial_shape) space_4d = ni.NeuroSpace.from_affine( affine, spatial_shape + (n_time,) ) reference = ni.DenseNeuroVol(np.ones(spatial_shape), space_3d) rois = { "seed": ni.cuboid_roi( reference, centroid=[1, 2, 2], surround=[0, 1, 1], fill=1 ), "strong": ni.cuboid_roi( reference, centroid=[3, 2, 2], surround=[0, 1, 1], fill=1 ), "moderate": ni.cuboid_roi( reference, centroid=[5, 2, 2], surround=[0, 1, 1], fill=1 ), "control": ni.cuboid_roi( reference, centroid=[3, 5, 2], surround=[0, 0, 1], fill=1 ), } motion = rng.normal(size=(n_time, 6)) seed_signal = rng.normal(size=n_time) data = rng.normal(scale=0.6, size=spatial_shape + (n_time,)) for name, coupling in { "seed": 1.0, "strong": 0.65, "moderate": 0.35, "control": 0.0, }.items(): coords = rois[name].coords data[tuple(coords.T)] += coupling * seed_signal + 0.4 * motion[:, 0] image = ni.DenseNeuroVec(data, space_4d) roi_results = { name: image.series_roi(roi) for name, roi in rois.items() } ``` ::: The extraction receipts make the boundary inspectable. Each result records the source-space hash, ROI mask hash, method, dimensions, and coordinates. The assertions verify that every extraction still points to the source affine and time axis. ::: {#711b0f0c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} assert all(result.n_timepoints == n_time for result in roi_results.values()) assert all( np.allclose(result.space.affine, affine) for result in roi_results.values() ) pd.DataFrame( [ { "ROI": name, "result": type(result).__name__, "time x voxels": str(result.values.shape), "method": result.provenance.method_name, "space receipt": result.provenance.source_affine_hash, "mask receipt": result.mask_hash, } for name, result in roi_results.items() ] ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
ROI result time x voxels method space receipt mask receipt
0 seed ROIExtractionResult (160, 9) series_roi e8fb69060af0df11 7ac60e9fa2a70232
1 strong ROIExtractionResult (160, 9) series_roi e8fb69060af0df11 d7ceeb6b36bb31bf
2 moderate ROIExtractionResult (160, 9) series_roi e8fb69060af0df11 73a858b9297d747d
3 control ROIExtractionResult (160, 3) series_roi e8fb69060af0df11 0e6f0ddc7dde67db
``` ::: ::: ## Build a dataset from pre-extracted ROI signals Connectivity operates on one representative series per ROI. We average the voxel series within each extraction result and keep the ROI names in a DataFrame. Only here, after spatial extraction and its receipts are visible, do those named series cross into fmrimod's matrix-backed dataset seam. This is pre-extracted ROI data, not flattened voxel data. ::: {#8767d7eb .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} roi_frame = pd.DataFrame( { name: result.values.mean(axis=1) for name, result in roi_results.items() } ) target_names = list(roi_frame.columns[1:]) dataset = fm.fmri_dataset(roi_frame.to_numpy(), tr=2.0) pd.DataFrame( { "runs": [dataset.n_runs], "time points": [dataset.n_timepoints], "ROI columns": [str(tuple(roi_frame.columns))], } ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
runs time points ROI columns
0 1 160 ('seed', 'strong', 'moderate', 'control')
``` ::: ::: ## Declare the nuisance model The drift, intercept, and motion confounds are a `baseline_model`, not a hand-assembled nuisance matrix. The model owns its column structure. ::: {#0be5841a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} bmodel = baseline_model( basis="poly", degree=2, sframe=dataset.sampling_frame, intercept="runwise", nuisance_list=[motion], ) design_matrix(bmodel).shape # (time, drift + intercept + motion columns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (160, 9) ``` ::: ::: ## Residualize through the model `residualize` dispatches on the model. Pass `bmodel` itself, not its matrix. This is the same projection the first-level seam uses, so the cleaned signal is consistent with how fmrimod fits everything else. ::: {#35204832 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} clean = residualize(bmodel, dataset.get_all_data()) clean.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (160, 4) ``` ::: ::: ## Seed-to-Target Correlation For a cleaned ROI matrix, the effect-size estimate is one explicit call. The helper preserves the readable "seed versus target columns" shape and adds Fisher-*z* columns for group-ready effect sizes. ::: {#8c6306f7 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} seed_target_correlation( clean, seed=0, target_names=target_names, ).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
target r n fisher_z z_variance
0 strong 0.931 160 1.664 0.006
1 moderate 0.815 160 1.142 0.006
2 control -0.017 160 -0.017 0.006
``` ::: ::: ## Seed as a GLM Covariate The fmrireg-style inferential version treats the seed time series as a sampled BOLD covariate. In fmrimod that is not a separate connectivity language: `covariate(...)` is an identity-HRF term, so it enters the same `fmri_lm` path as an ordinary authored model term. ::: {#20c82cb8 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} seed_source = pd.DataFrame({"seed": clean[:, 0]}) target_events = pd.DataFrame({ "onset": [0.0], "duration": [0.0], "trial_type": ["seed"], "run": [1], }) target_dataset = fm.fmri_dataset(clean[:, 1:2], tr=2.0, events=target_events) seed_fit = fm.fmri_lm(covariate("seed", source=seed_source), target_dataset) seed_index = seed_fit.design_columns().names.index("seed") round(float(seed_fit.coef()[seed_index, 0]), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 0.605 ``` ::: ::: For the common many-target ROI table, `seed_target_lm` is the compact helper on that same idea: it fits each target on `[intercept, confounds, seed]` and reports the seed coefficient, standard error, *t*, and *p*. ::: {#3f680da8 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} seed_target_lm( dataset.get_all_data(), seed=0, confounds=design_matrix(bmodel), add_intercept=False, target_names=target_names, ).to_frame().round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
target estimate se t p df
0 strong 0.605 0.019 31.190 0.000 150.0
1 moderate 0.299 0.017 17.233 0.000 150.0
2 control -0.007 0.032 -0.214 0.831 150.0
``` ::: ::: ## Back to fmrimod for Group-Ready Effect Sizes `seed_target_correlation` already includes the Fisher *z* and sampling variance `1 / (n - 3)`, which is exactly what the group seam (`fmri_meta`, `group_fit`) expects per connection. The lower-level `r_to_z` helper remains available when you already have correlations from another source. ::: {#71316d0f .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fc = seed_target_correlation(clean, seed=0) z = fc["fisher_z"].to_numpy() z_var = fc["z_variance"].to_numpy() pooled_r = fm.z_to_r(z.mean()) pd.DataFrame({ "fisher_z": z, "z_variance": z_var, }).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
fisher_z z_variance
0 1.664 0.006
1 1.142 0.006
2 -0.017 0.006
``` ::: ::: ::: {#f68383d0 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} round(float(z.mean()), 3), round(float(pooled_r), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` (0.93, 0.73) ``` ::: ::: The `strong` and `moderate` targets carry the planted correlations, while the `control` target stays near zero after nuisance removal. Fisher *z* and its variance are now in the form the group-level tools expect, so a connectivity result can flow into the same second-level analysis as any other effect. ## Next - [Group analysis](group-analysis.qmd) - [Datasets](datasets.qmd)
